nameStory: Mexican Stonecrop gets its name from its origins in Mexico and its incredible ability to grow on rocks and in thin, poor soils where most plants would struggle. The 'stonecrop' part comes from the Old English word 'crop,' meaning a sprout or young shoot that seems to magically emerge from stone crevices. It's also called 'Lemon Coral' because of its bright yellow-green foliage that resembles branching coral formations.
description: Mexican Stonecrop is a low-growing succulent plant that forms dense, spreading mats of thick, fleshy stems. This creeping perennial rarely grows taller than 3-4 inches but can spread widely across the ground. Its tiny, needle-like leaves are bright yellow-green and densely packed along trailing stems that root wherever they touch soil. Like other stonecrops, it produces small star-shaped flowers, though it's primarily grown for its colorful, coral-like foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, thick, needle-like leaves about 1/4 inch long that feel plump and watery when squeezed, arranged densely along the stems in a spiral pattern with a distinctive bright yellow-green color

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that creep along the ground with trailing stems that root at joints, creating a carpet-like appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Fleshy, succulent stems that feel firm and slightly rubbery to the touch, often reddish where exposed to bright sun

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow star-shaped flowers with 5 petals that appear in clusters at stem tips, though flowering is uncommon in New England's climate

habitat: Mexican Stonecrop is extremely rare in New England, with only 2 recorded observations, likely from garden escapes or deliberate plantings. When found, it grows in well-drained, sandy or rocky soils in full sun locations such as rock gardens, stone walls, or disturbed areas. It prefers poor, dry soils and cannot tolerate wet or heavy clay conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges bright yellow-green as temperatures warm, with stems beginning to spread and root at nodes where they contact soil.
seasonality.summer: Foliage reaches peak color intensity and the plant spreads most actively, though it may struggle in New England's humid summers.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows and stems may take on reddish tints, particularly where exposed to direct sunlight and cool temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Plant is not reliably hardy in New England winters and typically dies back or survives only in very protected microclimates.

funFact: Mexican Stonecrop can survive being completely dried out for weeks - you can literally pull up a piece, leave it on a windowsill until it's crispy, then stick it back in soil where it will plump up and start growing again like a plant zombie coming back to life!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small stonecrops, but Mexican Stonecrop's distinctive bright yellow-green 'lemon' color and coral-like branching pattern sets it apart from the more common gray-green or blue-green stonecrops. Remember: 'lemon-colored leaves, coral-shaped colonies.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it belongs in Mexico, this plant is widely used in temperate rock gardens and green roof applications worldwide, though it's not reliably winter-hardy in most of New England. The extremely low observation count suggests it doesn't naturalize here and any sightings are likely from recent garden plantings or greenhouse escapes.
compareHints: Mexican Stonecrop stands out from other New England stonecrops by its bright yellow-green 'lemon coral' coloration, while Stringy Stonecrop is more blue-green and Biting Stonecrop has shorter, more tightly packed triangular leaves. Unlike the hardier woodland stonecrop with its three-leaf clusters, Mexican Stonecrop has tiny needle-like leaves spiraling around the stems and lacks reliable winter hardiness in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike biting stonecrop which has tiny needle-like leaves that taste peppery, stringy stonecrop has larger, flatter leaves in groups of three that are essentially tasteless.
Among New England stonecrops, biting stonecrop has the smallest, most tightly overlapping leaves and the most intense golden-yellow flowers.
Among New England's stonecrops, white stonecrop stands out for its pure white flowers and cylindrical leaves that look like tiny green hot dogs.
Tasteless stonecrop's six-spiral leaf arrangement sets it apart from most other stonecrops in New England.
Woodland stonecrop stands out from its stonecrop relatives by its preference for shade and its unique four-petaled white flowers – most other Sedum species have five yellow petals and love full sun.
Among New England's stonecrops, Spanish stonecrop is distinguished by its particularly dense, mat-forming growth and tendency toward reddish stem coloration.

Unlike the common yellow-flowered biting stonecrop or the shade-loving woodland stonecrop with its distinctive three-leaf clusters, cliff stonecrop has pure white flowers and distinctly blue-green (glaucous) leaves.
Unlike the yellow-flowered biting stonecrop with its pointed, cone-shaped leaves, thick-leaved stonecrop has white or pink flowers and much plumper, rounder leaves.
Makino's stonecrop differs from Stringy Stonecrop by its more compact, less trailing growth habit and smaller stature.
